target.title: Speech Reconstruction from Silent Tongue and Lip Articulation By Pseudo Target Generation and Domain Adversarial Training

read.pdf: Fig. 1–3 and Tables 1–2 (read from the supplied text extraction; separate PDF not supplied)

entries.text: The paper proposes DTW-based pseudo acoustic targets to train speech reconstruction from silent articulation without natural silent speech labels.
entries.condition: Pseudo targets are generated from paired vocalized and silent recordings with the same linguistic content.
entries.quote: To solve this problem, we propose to generate pseudo acoustic targets for silent articulation so that the same supervised learning paradigm can be employed as in the vocalized mode.

entries.text: The proposed domain-adversarial training combines silent and vocalized data to learn representations invariant across the two domains.
entries.condition: Joint training uses silent pseudo-target reconstruction, vocalized reconstruction, and a domain discriminator.
entries.quote: To address this issue, domain adversarial training is introduced into the model to force the encoder to learn more robust articulatory representations invariant in both silent and vocalized domains.

entries.text: The method iteratively regenerates pseudo targets with the updated domain-adversarial encoder to improve target quality.
entries.condition: After some training epochs, pseudo targets and the reliable-sample threshold are recomputed.

entries.text: The authors identify TaLNet as the state-of-the-art vocalized tongue-and-lip speech reconstruction model on TaL and use it as their baseline.
entries.condition: The cited state-of-the-art designation is limited to vocalized tongue-and-lip input on the TaL dataset.

entries.text: TaLNet has parallel ultrasound-tongue and optical-lip sub-encoders; their frame vectors are concatenated and linearly projected.
entries.condition: Input consists of tongue ultrasound images and lip video; each sub-encoder uses stacked 3D CNNs.

entries.text: The acoustic decoder is transferred from Tacotron2, uses forced attention, autoregressive acoustic prediction, a 2-layer LSTM, and CNN post-processing.
entries.condition: The decoder is jointly trained with the TaLNet encoder after transfer from a multi-speaker TTS model.

entries.text: A pretrained TaLNet encoder aligns same-content silent and vocalized articulatory representations with DTW; the vocalized natural acoustic features are warped to form silent pseudo targets.
entries.condition: Parallel recordings from the two speaking modes are required; the initial alignment uses the vocalized-trained TaLNet encoder.
entries.quote: Then we propose to perform dynamic time warping (DTW) [18] to align the encoder output Fv in the source vocalised domain to Fs in the target silent domain.

entries.text: Only silent training examples whose DTW alignment cost is below threshold epsilon contribute to pseudo-target reconstruction loss.
entries.condition: The set of selected examples is recomputed as the encoder and representation scale change.
entries.quote: The cost of DTW alignment is employed as the criterion of selecting reliable samples.

entries.text: The domain discriminator receives randomly sampled encoder segments concatenated before CNN, max-pooling, linear, and softmax classification.
entries.condition: Segments are randomly drawn from encoder outputs of different lengths; discriminator predicts silent versus vocalized domain.
entries.quote: Therefore, 32 segments with a length of 50 frames are randomly selected from the output of the encoder, spliced together, and sent to the domain discriminator for classiﬁcation.

entries.text: The adversarial-loss weight lambda is increased from zero using the Ganin schedule based on current and total epochs.
entries.condition: A gradient reversal layer applies the negative discriminator loss to the encoder.

entries.text: For the first 50 epochs the encoder updates every five batches and discriminator every batch; later their update frequencies are switched.
entries.value: 50 epochs; encoder every 5 batches then every batch; discriminator every batch then every 5 batches
entries.condition: The change applies to domain-adversarial model training.

entries.text: Three iterative-training rounds use DTW cost thresholds of 40 in round one and 49 in rounds two and three, chosen heuristically from mean training-sample costs.
entries.condition: Thresholds apply to selecting reliable silent training examples and are revised as representations change.

entries.text: Eighteen speakers whose silent-utterance DTW costs all exceeded the first-round threshold were excluded from the silent-mode test set.
entries.condition: The TaL corpus has 81 speakers; exclusion was applied to all silent-mode models in the following experiments, not to the vocalized test set as described.
entries.quote: There were 18 speakers whose DTW costs of all silent utterances were above the threshold in the ﬁrst iteration.

entries.text: TaL supplies synchronized audio, ultrasound tongue images, and lip video in vocalized and silent modes from native English speakers.
entries.condition: Dataset is Tongue and Lip (TaL); the paper reports both speaking modes and synchronized modalities.
entries.quote: It contains synchronized audio, ultrasound tongue images, and lip videos in both vocalized and silent speaking modes from 81 native English speakers.

entries.text: The corpus contains 1,212 silent utterances, each paired with a same-linguistic-content vocalized utterance; speakers have about 15 silent utterances each.
entries.condition: TaL dataset; pairings are across silent and vocalized modes.
entries.quote: There are 1212 utterances in the silent speaking mode in the corpus, each with a corresponding vocalized utterance with the same linguistic content.

entries.text: Two utterances were randomly selected from each speaker for validation and test respectively, with the remaining utterances assigned to training; the wording does not make per-split allocation explicit.
entries.value: 2 selected utterances per speaker, allocation between validation and test not explicit
entries.condition: Utterance-level random split; remaining silent utterances are training data.
entries.quote: 2 utterances were randomly selected from each speaker to form the validation set and the test set respectively

entries.text: Domain-adversarial training uses only vocalized utterances with the same linguistic content as silent articulations; the vocalized test set has one utterance per speaker and is utterance-disjoint from vocalized training for both systems.
entries.condition: For domain-adversarial training only same-linguistic-content vocalized utterances are selected; test utterance is stated not to overlap the vocalized training set of pretrained TaLNet or the proposed method, but speaker-level disjointness is not claimed.

entries.text: The adopted TaLNet baseline was pretrained on 11,487 vocalized TaL utterances.
entries.condition: TaLNet model built in prior work [13]; used as the baseline and as the pretrained encoder for first-iteration pseudo-target generation.

entries.text: The proposed system is evaluated without speaker-dependent fine-tuning; the TaLNet baseline is likewise evaluated without speaker-dependent fine-tuning.
entries.condition: This is the paper's meaning of speaker-independent; the utterance-level split described in Sec. 4.1 still samples train, validation, and test utterances from each speaker.

entries.text: The model predicts acoustic features/mel spectrograms from articulation; a Parallel WaveGAN vocoder synthesizes the speech waveform.
entries.condition: Silent and vocalized articulatory input; the same TaLNet architecture is used, with PWG waveform synthesis.

entries.text: Objective evaluation uses MCD, STOI, and ASR WER; silent-mode MCD/STOI compare against PWG waveforms made from generated pseudo acoustic features because no silent ground-truth speech exists.
entries.condition: MCD/STOI reference for silent test utterances is synthetic pseudo-target speech, not naturally recorded silent speech; WER is from the iFLYTEK ASR API.
entries.quote: Since there was no ground truth speech for the silent utterances

entries.text: The natural vocalized test recordings have mean ASR WER 4.110%; the pseudo-reference speech for silent test utterances has mean WER 10.246%.
entries.condition: Reference WERs reported for vocalized natural recordings and PWG-vocoded pseudo-reference speech, respectively, on the paper's test sets using iFLYTEK ASR.
entries.quote: the mean WER of all the vocalized natural recordings in the test set was 4.110%

entries.text: Silent-mode TaLNet baseline results: MCD 4.423, STOI 0.432, WER 59.960, MOS 2.990 ± 0.123.
entries.unit: MCD dB; STOI; WER %; MOS on 5-point scale (95% CI)
entries.condition: Table 1 means on the silent test set; 18 speakers excluded for high first-round DTW costs; no speaker-dependent fine-tuning. MCD/STOI use PWG-vocoded pseudo references; WER uses iFLYTEK ASR; MOS protocol is 21 native English MTurk listeners and 15 sampled utterances per system/mode.

entries.text: Silent-mode proposed-method results: MCD 3.935, STOI 0.517, WER 43.114, MOS 3.330 ± 0.120.
entries.unit: MCD dB; STOI; WER %; MOS on 5-point scale (95% CI)
entries.condition: Table 1 means on the silent test set; 18 speakers excluded for high first-round DTW costs; no speaker-dependent fine-tuning. MCD/STOI use PWG-vocoded pseudo references; WER uses iFLYTEK ASR; MOS protocol is 21 native English MTurk listeners and 15 sampled utterances per system/mode.

entries.text: Vocalized-mode TaLNet baseline results: MCD 3.421, STOI 0.666, WER 26.890, MOS 3.421 ± 0.122.
entries.unit: MCD dB; STOI; WER %; MOS on 5-point scale (95% CI)
entries.condition: Table 1 means on the vocalized test set, with one test utterance per speaker and utterance-level non-overlap with vocalized training; no speaker-dependent fine-tuning. WER uses iFLYTEK ASR; MOS protocol is 21 native English MTurk listeners and 15 sampled utterances per system/mode.

entries.text: Vocalized-mode proposed-method results: MCD 3.382, STOI 0.684, WER 17.309, MOS 3.672 ± 0.109.
entries.unit: MCD dB; STOI; WER %; MOS on 5-point scale (95% CI)
entries.condition: Table 1 means on the vocalized test set, with one test utterance per speaker and utterance-level non-overlap with vocalized training; no speaker-dependent fine-tuning. WER uses iFLYTEK ASR; MOS protocol is 21 native English MTurk listeners and 15 sampled utterances per system/mode.

entries.text: Vocalized ground-truth comparison is vocoder-resynthesized natural speech with MOS 4.161 ± 0.096; objective metrics are not reported for this row.
entries.condition: Table 1 GT is natural vocalized speech resynthesized by the vocoder; MOS listening-test protocol is described in Sec. 4.3.

entries.text: The abstract claims silent-mode WER decreases by over 15% versus TaLNet and that intelligibility and naturalness improve.
entries.unit: % WER decrease (paper does not specify relative percent versus percentage points in this sentence)
entries.condition: Silent speaking mode compared with baseline TaLNet; test-set protocol and scores are in Table 1.
entries.quote: When using an automatic speech recognition (ASR) model to measure intelligibility, the word error rate (WER) of our proposed method decreases by over 15% compared to the baseline.

entries.text: The abstract also claims vocalized-mode WER falls by approximately 10% against TaLNet.
entries.unit: % WER decrease (paper does not specify relative percent versus percentage points in this sentence)
entries.condition: Vocalized articulating mode compared with baseline TaLNet; test-set protocol and scores are in Table 1.
entries.quote: In addition, our proposed method also outperforms the baseline on the intelligibility of the speech reconstructed in vocalized articulating mode, reducing the WER by approximately 10%.

entries.text: Authors report a silent-mode MOS increase of 0.34 with paired t-test p = 2.11 × 10^-6.
entries.condition: Proposed method versus TaLNet on the silent test-set listening evaluation; 5-point MOS, 21 native English MTurk listeners, 15 sampled utterances per system/mode.

entries.text: Each mode's subjective test recruited 21 native English MTurk raters, used a 5-point scale, and randomly sampled 15 utterances generated by each system in that mode.
entries.value: 21 raters per test; 5 rating points; 15 utterances per system per mode
entries.condition: Two mode-specific listening tests; the paper does not state the number of judgments per clip or whether all raters rated all sampled utterances.

entries.text: Silent-mode ablation without iterative training reports MCD 3.971, STOI 0.512, and WER 46.016.
entries.condition: Table 2 silent test set; 18 high-DTW-cost speakers excluded; no speaker-dependent fine-tuning; MCD/STOI against PWG-vocoded pseudo references and WER by iFLYTEK ASR.

entries.text: Silent-mode ablation without domain-adversarial training reports MCD 4.009, STOI 0.51, and WER 51.199.
entries.condition: Table 2 silent test set; 18 high-DTW-cost speakers excluded; no speaker-dependent fine-tuning; MCD/STOI against PWG-vocoded pseudo references and WER by iFLYTEK ASR.

entries.text: Vocalized-mode ablation without iterative training reports MCD 3.392, STOI 0.683, and WER 18.122.
entries.condition: Table 2 vocalized test set, one utterance per speaker and utterance-disjoint from vocalized training; no speaker-dependent fine-tuning; WER by iFLYTEK ASR.

entries.text: Vocalized-mode ablation without domain-adversarial training reports MCD 3.434, STOI 0.670, and WER 25.032.
entries.condition: Table 2 vocalized test set, one utterance per speaker and utterance-disjoint from vocalized training; no speaker-dependent fine-tuning; WER by iFLYTEK ASR.

entries.text: Authors state both ablations underperform the full method on every objective metric in both modes, while still outperforming TaLNet on those metrics.
entries.condition: Objective metrics are MCD, STOI, and WER on the test sets in Tables 1–2; silent test excludes 18 speakers.

entries.text: Silent-mode test WER across the three training iterations is 46.016, 44.002, and 43.114%.
entries.condition: Figure 2 silent test set, after excluding 18 high-DTW-cost speakers; same model/test conditions as the proposed system.
entries.quote: The test set WERs at different training iterations of our proposed method.

entries.text: Vocalized-mode test WER across the three training iterations is 18.122, 17.967, and 17.309%.
entries.condition: Figure 2 vocalized test set; one test utterance per speaker and utterance-disjoint from vocalized training.

entries.text: The plotted least-squares fit for speaker-wise WER is y = 0.81x - 0.03; the authors characterize the relation as strongly positive.
entries.unit: linear fit; x/y are TaLNet/proposed-method WER (%)
entries.condition: Figure 3 fits speaker-wise silent-mode WER comparisons; no correlation coefficient, interval, or significance test is reported.

entries.text: Authors attribute vocalized-mode improvements partly to DTW pseudo-labels acting as data augmentation and to domain-invariant representations improving generalization to unseen vocalized articulation.
entries.condition: Proposed explanation for the vocalized test results; generalization mechanism is stated as a possibility, not isolated by a dedicated experiment.
entries.quote: the domain discriminator makes the encoder concentrate on deriving domain-invariant articulatory representations, which may also improve the generalization ability of the model when dealing with unseen vocalized articulation data.

entries.text: The authors concede that speech reconstruction still has a clear performance gap between silent and vocalized modes and leave modeling intrinsic articulation differences to future work.
entries.condition: Conclusion; applies to the proposed articulatory-to-acoustic conversion framework.

entries.text: Authors suspect some speakers produced unreliable silent articulation and exclude those speakers from all subsequent silent-mode tests based on DTW costs.
entries.condition: The exclusion rule applies to the 18 speakers whose every silent-utterance DTW cost exceeded the first-iteration threshold.
entries.quote: We suspected that these speakers may have unreliable silent articulations and thus excluded them from the test set for all silent-mode models in following experiments.

entries.text: The authors note substantial speaker-wise WER variation and suggest that some speakers may not articulate correctly without audio feedback, limiting intelligibility improvement.
entries.condition: Discussion of speaker-wise silent-mode reconstruction results; stated as a possible explanation.

entries.text: The paper does not report random seeds for data partitioning, segment sampling, MOS utterance sampling, initialization, or training, nor independent-run repetitions for objective results.
entries.condition: Random selection is explicitly used for split, discriminator segments, and MOS samples, but seed and repeated-run policy are absent.
entries.quote: 2 utterances were randomly selected from each speaker to form the validation set and the test set respectively

entries.text: Session-level train/validation/test allocation and session overlap are not reported.
entries.condition: The dataset split is described by utterance and speaker only; no session identifiers or session-based partition protocol are given.

entries.text: The exact number of utterances assigned to validation versus test per speaker is ambiguous, and the checkpoint or hyperparameter selection procedure using validation data is not reported.
entries.condition: The paper states that two utterances per speaker were selected for validation and test respectively but does not specify their allocation or how validation results affected model selection.

entries.text: Speakers occur across train, validation, and test utterances; the protocol is not speaker-disjoint despite the authors' use of speaker-independent to mean no speaker-dependent fine-tuning (inference).
entries.condition: Each speaker contributes randomly selected validation/test utterances and remaining training utterances; vocalized test utterances are stated to be utterance-disjoint from vocalized training, not speaker-disjoint.
entries.quote: 2 utterances were randomly selected from each speaker to form the validation set and the test set respectively

entries.text: The iFLYTEK ASR API model/version, language configuration, decoding settings, vocabulary or lexicon, language-model use, and text normalization/tokenization used for WER are not specified.
entries.unit: ASR decoding and WER normalization conditions
entries.condition: WER is reported for reconstructed speech using the named iFLYTEK API; no service version or recognition configuration is provided.
entries.quote: the iFLYTEK speech recognition API 2 was employed to measure the WERs of different models.

entries.text: Input feature normalization and detailed MCD/STOI implementations or parameter settings are not reported.
entries.condition: Objective metrics are named, but feature scaling, normalization statistics, MCD configuration, and STOI implementation settings are not specified.

entries.text: No chance-level or other explicit chance benchmark is reported for the speech reconstruction evaluation.
entries.condition: Objective evaluation reports MCD, STOI, WER and subjective MOS; the paper gives natural/reference recordings but no chance-level score.

entries.text: The paper does not specify rater blinding, presentation order, number of ratings per utterance, or the exact sampling frame for the 15 MOS utterances.
entries.condition: Twenty-one raters per mode-specific test and 15 randomly selected utterances per system per mode are reported.

entries.text: No online deployment, latency, throughput, hardware, or real-world assistive-use evaluation is reported.
entries.condition: The study reports offline corpus experiments and waveform generation only.

entries.text: The reported mean ASR WER of the PWG-vocoded pseudo-reference speech for silent test utterances is 10.246%.
entries.condition: Reference speech for silent test utterances is synthesized from generated pseudo acoustic features with PWG; iFLYTEK ASR is used.
entries.quote: mentioned above was 10.246%.

entries.text: Each speaker has about 15 silent-mode utterances in TaL.
entries.condition: TaL dataset; 81 native English speakers; used to motivate per-speaker random validation/test sampling.

entries.text: DTW cost thresholds were 40 in iteration one and 49 in each of the next two iterations.
entries.condition: Thresholds select reliable silent training samples; authors chose them heuristically from mean DTW cost across training samples.

entries.text: MOS sampling randomly selected 15 generated utterances per system in each speaking mode.
entries.condition: Subjective listening evaluation; 21 native English raters were recruited for each mode-specific test.

entries.text: Table 1 reports means on the test set and indicates that plus/minus values are 95% confidence intervals.
entries.condition: Table 1; intervals are shown for MOS values.

entries.text: The authors state that the proposed method outperforms TaLNet on all objective and subjective metrics in silent mode.
entries.condition: Silent-mode comparison on Table 1 test set; objective MCD/STOI use synthetic pseudo-reference speech and WER uses iFLYTEK ASR.

entries.text: The authors state that the proposed method significantly improves naturalness and intelligibility in vocalized-mode reconstruction over TaLNet.
entries.condition: Vocalized test set described in Sec. 4.1; one utterance per speaker and utterance-level non-overlap with vocalized training.

entries.text: No uncertainty intervals or statistical significance tests are reported for objective MCD, STOI, or WER comparisons; the only reported paired test is for silent-mode MOS.
entries.condition: Table 1 presents objective means without interval notation; its ± confidence intervals apply to MOS values.

entries.text: The w/o ITS ablation performs pseudo-target generation and domain-adversarial model training only once.
entries.condition: Table 2 ablation; applied in silent and vocalized modes.

entries.text: The w/o DAT ablation removes the domain discriminator and reduces the loss to silent pseudo-target reconstruction loss.
entries.condition: Table 2 ablation in both modes; the stated reduction is to LRecon,s.
entries.quote: For “w/o DAT” , Eq. (3) degraded to LRecon,s without using the domain discriminator.

entries.text: The specific natural or synthetic reference signal used for vocalized-mode MCD and STOI is not explicitly identified.
entries.condition: Sec. 4.3 explicitly defines the pseudo-reference for silent MCD/STOI but does not separately state the vocalized MCD/STOI comparator.

entries.text: The overall loss is the silent pseudo-target loss plus the vocalized reconstruction loss minus the weighted discriminator loss; training is joint over silent and vocalized data.
entries.quote: our method performs joint training on both silent and vocalized articulation data

entries.text: The paper does not state which model or encoder iteration produced the pseudo acoustic features of the test silent utterances that serve as the MCD/STOI reference.
entries.condition: Sec. 4.3 says only that the generated pseudo acoustic features of test utterances were vocoded by PWG.
entries.quote: the generated pseudo acoustic features of test utterances were input to the PWG vocoder

entries.text: Silent-mode MCD and STOI are computed against PWG waveforms generated from the pseudo acoustic features of the test utterances.
entries.condition: Silent test set; no natural silent-mode speech exists.
entries.quote: the generated pseudo acoustic features of test utterances were input to the PWG vocoder to generate waveforms

entries.text: Pseudo targets are generated by aligning encoder outputs of the vocalized and silent recordings, not raw articulatory or acoustic features.
entries.condition: Initial alignment uses the encoder of the vocalized-trained TaLNet.
entries.quote: align the encoder output Fv in the source vocalised domain to Fs in the target silent domain

entries.text: Gaddy and Klein transfer vocalized audio targets to silent EMG by DTW, refine with CCA, then realign with predicted audio from the partially trained model, recomputing alignments every five epochs.
entries.condition: Single-speaker EMG corpus; open-vocabulary condition.
entries.quote: From then on, we re-compute alignments every ﬁve epochs

entries.text: Initial alignment uses DTW between EMG signals, refined with CCA and predicted audio.
entries.condition: Training targets for silent EMG
entries.quote: The alignment is initially found using dynamic time warping between EMG signals

entries.text: Open-vocabulary automatic WER: full model 68.0, without predicted-audio realignment 76.5.
entries.condition: Table 5, open vocabulary, DeepSpeech automatic transcription, silent EMG
entries.quote: Without audio alignment 76.5

entries.text: Gaddy and Klein also train on vocalized EMG, label it with different session embeddings so the model can specialize per mode, and mix both modes in each batch.
entries.condition: Pooled silent and vocalized training
entries.quote: The vocalized samples are labeled with different session embeddings to allow the model to specialize to each speaking mode

entries.text: Removing the non-parallel vocalized recordings raises WER to 71.6%, 3.6 points worse.
entries.condition: Open vocabulary, automatic transcription
entries.quote: A model trained without this data has a WER of 71.6%, a loss of 3.6 absolute percentage points

entries.text: Silent outputs are evaluated by transcription WER (human and automatic) against the prompt text; ASR on the vocalized test audio gives 9.5% WER as a lower bound.
entries.condition: Open vocabulary; DeepSpeech
entries.quote: results in a WER of 9.5%, which represents a lower bound for this evaluation

entries.text: The Gaddy corpus has nearly 20 hours of facial EMG from a single speaker.
entries.condition: Single speaker

entries.text: Janke and Diener align the audible recording to silent EMG with DTW to obtain acoustic targets for silent EMG-to-speech.
entries.condition: EMG-Array-AS-200 corpus, audible and silent data per session
entries.quote: we can use the acoustic data and align this data to the silent EMG data using DTW

entries.text: Domain-adversarial training with a speaker classifier makes a lipreading network confuse speakers.
entries.condition: GRID lipreading, speaker domains
entries.quote: causes the joint part of the network to learn to confuse speakers instead of separating them

entries.text: Domain-adversarial training adapts an EMG recognizer frontend to a new recording session without supervised enrollment.
entries.condition: EMG continuous speech recognition, session domains
entries.quote: we present a system which adapts the neural network frontend of our recognizer to data from a new recording session

entries.text: A silent-voiced representation alignment loss lowers silent EMG-to-speech WER from 26.75% to 25.14% against Gaddy's model, p = 0.002.
entries.condition: Gaddy corpus silent test, mean over 10 seeds
entries.quote: yielding a relative WER reduction of 6.0% (from 26.75% to 25.14%)

entries.text: Lee et al. train with 10 seeds.
entries.condition: Multi-seed protocol
entries.quote: we trained the model with 10 different seeds for 200 epochs each

entries.text: GETS reaches 11.89% WER on the silent EMG test set.
entries.condition: Gaddy corpus silent EMG test set
entries.quote: Word Error Rate (WER) of 11.89% on the silent EMG test set

entries.text: On the same TaL corpus, Ribeiro et al. train recognizers on modal speech and address the silent-mode mismatch with fMLLR and unsupervised model adaptation.
entries.condition: TaL ultrasound and lip video recognition
entries.quote: using techniques that address the domain mismatch, such as fMLLR and unsupervised model adaptation

entries.text: No discriminator accuracy, representation distance or visualization of domain invariance is reported; the text contains no 'accuracy', 'distance' or 't-SNE' (checked Secs. 1-5).
entries.condition: Domain-adversarial training, Secs. 3.2, 4.3, 4.4
entries.quote: domain adversarial training is introduced into the model to force the encoder to learn more robust articulatory representations invariant in both silent and vocalized domains

entries.condition: Table 5, open vocabulary, automatic transcription

questions.q: Do the silent-mode objective scores compare reconstructed speech against naturally recorded silent speech?
questions.answer: No. The paper says no ground-truth speech exists for silent utterances and uses PWG-vocoded pseudo acoustic features as the MCD/STOI reference; the reference's reported ASR WER is 10.246%. The benchmark limitation follows from the reported protocol (inference).

questions.q: Does the evaluation test generalization to speakers absent from training?
questions.answer: No speaker-disjoint split is described: utterances from each speaker are divided among training, validation, and test, while speaker-independent refers to the absence of speaker-dependent fine-tuning (inference).

questions.q: Gaddy & Klein 2020: how are silent targets built, how often are alignments recomputed, and how are silent outputs evaluated? Target: who produced the test pseudo references, and what remains in w/o DAT?
questions.answer: DTW on EMG, CCA, then predicted-audio realignment recomputed every five epochs; Table 5 68.0 vs 76.5 without audio alignment; vocalized data pooled with mode-specific session embeddings; silent outputs scored by transcription WER only. Target does not say which encoder made the test pseudo references; w/o DAT keeps only LRecon,s (LRecon,v dropped).
